aim: Explain why 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 is False in Python because floats are stored in binary, compare floats safely with math.isclose or an explicit tolerance, and round with round() or an f-string only for display.
approach: Start from the surprise itself, then explain it with an analogy the learner already knows (1/3 cannot be written exactly in decimal, and 1/10 cannot be written exactly in binary), and make it visible by printing the exact value Python really stores for 0.1. Then give two separate tools for two separate jobs, a tolerance for comparing and rounding for display, so the learner knows which to reach for and why rounding the stored number is not the same as comparing it. The rules are shown by running small programs, so the learner can rebuild the explanation instead of memorising 'never use == on floats'.
bridge: Python has two main number types. An int such as 3 is a whole number and is exact, however large it gets. A float such as 3.0 or 0.1 has a fractional part and is only stored approximately. Writing a decimal point makes a float, so 3 and 3.0 are different types: print(type(3), type(3.0)) shows <class 'int'> <class 'float'>. The / operator always gives a float (6 / 3 is 2.0), while // gives a whole-number quotient (7 // 2 is 3) and % gives the remainder (7 % 2 is 1). An int combined with a float gives a float (1 + 0.5 is 1.5). That is all this lesson needs from numbers; keep it to a few lines with one tiny program and its output.

sections.title: The surprise: 0.1 + 0.2
sections.teach: Show that the arithmetic looks wrong and that this is not a bug in the learner's code. Print 0.1 + 0.2 and the comparison 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3. Print the difference (0.1 + 0.2) - 0.3, which is tiny but not zero. Contrast with 1 + 2 == 3, which is True because ints are exact. State plainly that Python is doing what it was designed to do, and that the same answer appears in JavaScript, Java, C and most other languages, because they all use the same standard for floats (IEEE 754, 64-bit 'double precision'). CPython uses the C double of the machine, which on essentially all current computers follows that standard. Note that the learner can check this themselves in any other language they have.
sections.example: A short program printing 0.1 + 0.2 (0.30000000000000004), 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 (False), (0.1 + 0.2) - 0.3 (5.551115123125783e-17) and 1 + 2 == 3 (True). Briefly explain that e-17 means times 10 to the power of minus 17, so the gap is about 0.0000000000000000555.

sections.title: Why: binary can't store 0.1 exactly
sections.teach: Build the explanation in steps. (1) In decimal, 1/3 is 0.3333... and never ends, so any written-down version is slightly off. This is a limit of the number system, not of the writer. (2) A computer stores a float in binary, with place values 1/2, 1/4, 1/8, 1/16 and so on. A fraction can be written exactly only if its denominator, in lowest terms, is a power of 2. So 0.5, 0.25 and 0.375 are exact, but 0.1 (which is 1/10) in binary repeats forever, like 0.0001100110011..., and has to be cut off after a fixed number of bits (a 64-bit float keeps 53 significant bits). (3) So the stored number is the nearest representable one, slightly above 0.1. Each of 0.1 and 0.2 carries a tiny error, the sum carries both, and the nearest float to the true sum is a different float from the nearest float to 0.3. Explain the thing that confuses most learners: print(0.1) shows 0.1 because Python prints the shortest text that turns back into the same float, not the full stored value, so the display hides the error. Make the stored value visible with Decimal(0.1). Explain briefly where it appears that Decimal comes from the decimal module in the standard library, that importing makes a tool available, and that Decimal(0.1) simply prints the exact value of the float it was given. Honest scope: this applies to values that are not sums of powers of 2, and values like 0.5 or 0.25 (and sums of them) are exact, so the problem is not 'all floats are wrong'.
sections.example: One program: from decimal import Decimal; print(Decimal(0.1)) giving 0.1000000000000000055511151231257827021181583404541015625; print(Decimal(0.5)) giving 0.5; print(format(0.1, '.20f')) giving 0.10000000000000000555 (explain that format(x, '.20f') asks for 20 digits after the point). Then 0.5 + 0.25 == 0.75 printing True, to show that exactly representable values add exactly. Also print(0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3) was False above, so connect: the error in 0.1 is about 5.55e-18, the stored 0.2 has twice that, and the sum lands one float step away from the stored 0.3.

sections.title: Errors add up
sections.teach: Show that the tiny error is not a one-off: repeating an operation lets it build up. Add 0.1 ten times in a loop (explain the loop in one line, 'repeat this 10 times'; the learner may not have met for loops yet) and compare with 1.0. Keep the claim modest: errors can grow or can cancel, and how large they get depends on the numbers and the order of the operations. Point out that this is the reason a test like total == 1.0 is fragile, and that the difference is still extremely small (around 1e-16), so the results are almost right, just not bit-for-bit equal.
sections.example: total = 0.0; for _ in range(10): total += 0.1; print(total) giving 0.9999999999999999; print(total == 1.0) giving False; print(abs(total - 1.0)) giving 1.1102230246251565e-16.

sections.title: Comparing floats safely
sections.teach: Replace == with 'close enough'. First by hand: abs(a - b) < tolerance, where abs gives the size of a number ignoring its sign, and the tolerance is a small number you choose (for example 1e-9, written in scientific notation). Then math.isclose(a, b), explaining that math is a standard-library module that must be imported. Explain relative tolerance in plain words: being off by 0.001 is huge for values near 0.001 but invisible for values near a billion, so isclose by default allows a difference of up to 1e-09 times the larger of the two values (rel_tol=1e-09). Then the honest edge case that surprises people and shows how the function works: when one value is 0, a relative tolerance of 'a billionth of the bigger value' is tiny, so isclose(1e-12, 0.0) is False. For comparisons near zero you must supply abs_tol, for example abs_tol=1e-9, which is a fixed allowed gap. Say that the right tolerance depends on the problem and there is no universal number; the defaults suit roughly 9 digits of agreement. Tell the learner they can check the exact defaults themselves with help(math.isclose) and in the Python documentation for the math module.
sections.example: One program printing 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 (False), abs((0.1 + 0.2) - 0.3) < 1e-9 (True), math.isclose(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3) (True), math.isclose(1e-12, 0.0) (False), math.isclose(1e-12, 0.0, abs_tol=1e-9) (True).

sections.title: Rounding is for display
sections.teach: Separate two ideas the learner may blur: what is stored versus what is shown. Use f'{x:.2f}' (explain in a sentence: an f-string puts a value into text, and :.2f means 'a float with 2 digits after the point'; the full story of f-strings is a separate point in this topic) and round(x, 2) to make output tidy, for example showing 0.1 + 0.2 as 0.30. Be clear that the f-string only changes the text, the number itself is unchanged, so (0.1 + 0.2) printed as 0.30 still fails == 0.3. round() returns a new float, which is itself again only the nearest representable float to a decimal, so round(x, 2) == 0.3 can work in this case but it is not a general substitute for a tolerance. Then the surprise that reveals the mechanism: round(2.675, 2) gives 2.67, not the 2.68 that school rounding suggests, because the float written 2.675 is actually stored just below 2.675, so it is not a tie at all; Decimal(2.675) shows this. Also mention, as a separate and genuine rule, that round() on an exact tie such as round(0.5) and round(2.5) rounds to the nearest even number (0 and 2), called banker's rounding, and say this is the documented behaviour of Python 3's round() and can be checked in help(round). Do not present either as a bug.
sections.example: One program printing the stored and displayed values: x = 0.1 + 0.2; print(x) giving 0.30000000000000004; print(f'{x:.2f}') giving 0.30; print(round(x, 2)) giving 0.3; print(x == 0.3) giving False; print(round(x, 2) == 0.3) giving True. Then print(round(2.675, 2)) giving 2.67 and print(Decimal(2.675)) showing a value just under 2.675 (the writer should show the exact digits only if it is certain of them, otherwise show format(2.675, '.20f') and state that the digits shown begin 2.67499999...).

sections.title: Which tool for which job
sections.teach: Close with a short, honest decision rule rather than a slogan: comparing two computed floats means a tolerance (math.isclose, or later numpy.isclose / numpy.allclose for arrays); showing a number to a reader means an f-string or round(); a value that must stay exactly decimal (money is the usual case) is a job for whole numbers of cents or for the Decimal type, which the learner can look up later. Say where '==' on floats is fine: comparing to a value you set directly with no arithmetic in between, and values that are exactly representable, but explain that it is safer to make the tolerance habit automatic when the numbers come out of calculations. Ask the learner to predict, then run, two or three small expressions (for example 0.5 + 0.25 == 0.75, 0.1 * 3 == 0.3, 1.1 + 2.2 == 3.3) before looking at the outputs, so they test the explanation on new cases.
sections.example: A final 'predict, then run' program with three comparisons and their outputs: 0.5 + 0.25 == 0.75 prints True; 0.1 * 3 == 0.3 prints False (0.1 * 3 is 0.30000000000000004); 1.1 + 2.2 == 3.3 prints False (1.1 + 2.2 is 3.3000000000000003). Then the same three written with math.isclose all print True.

beyond: Where the rules stop holding: ints are exact (Python ints have no fixed size limit), and only floats carry this error; a float has about 15 to 17 significant decimal digits, and the gap between neighbouring floats grows with the size of the number, so beyond 2**53 (about 9.0e15) a float can no longer tell consecutive whole numbers apart (2.0**53 + 1 == 2.0**53 is True). Addition of floats is not always associative, so the order of summing can change the last digits (math.fsum sums more accurately). Underneath: a 64-bit float is one sign bit, 11 exponent bits and 52 stored fraction bits, which works like scientific notation in binary; sys.float_info.epsilon (2.220446049250313e-16) is the gap between 1.0 and the next float. These deserve a proper extension after the lesson because the learner can observe them directly: float.hex() (for instance (0.1).hex() prints 0x1.999999999999ap-4, the repeating 1001 pattern cut off and rounded), Decimal(x) for the exact stored value, and sys.float_info. Of this, I am certain of the 1/11/52 layout and the epsilon value, which can be checked in the Python tutorial section 'Floating-Point Arithmetic: Issues and Limitations' and the documentation for the sys and math modules; the textbook pointers on the map were recalled from memory by an AI and I have not checked their chapter numbers. Also worth a short mention in the next lesson: float32 (used by many ML libraries) has far fewer digits than Python's float, and NaN (not a number) breaks == in a different way, since nan == nan is False; that is the next point (NaN and infinity in arrays) and should not be explained here beyond one sentence.
goal_link: In machine learning with NumPy, pandas and scikit-learn, nearly every number is a float, so you will meet this when checking that two arrays or a model's outputs match (np.isclose and np.allclose are the array versions of math.isclose), when a computed total or accuracy prints with a long tail of digits, and when you format results for display.
